title: Checkpoint: Reality, Time and God
objective: After this level you can connect puzzles about reality, time and God's existence to the earlier chapters' tools of reason and experience.
summary: This chapter’s arguments about reality, time and God start from reason alone or from the observed world, and critics often reply with the other tool, as Chapter 1’s schools debated.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: reality, time and God, sorted.
cards.body: Some of these arguments start from what you can see. Others start from reason alone. Sorting them that way is the chapter’s big lesson.

cards.headline: Reason alone, or the world first?

items.label: From reason alone
points: Anselm: the greatest conceivable being must exist
Zeno: a proof that Achilles never catches the tortoise
Plato: the Good, seen last, known by thought

items.label: From the world first
points: Al-Ghazali and Aquinas: chains of causes
Paley: parts fitted for a purpose, watch to eye
Augustine: time found in memory and expectation

cards.headline: Critics swap tools
cards.body: Replies often reach for the other tool. Against inborn knowledge of Plato’s Forms, Locke insisted knowledge comes from experience. Against Anselm, Kant argued existence isn’t something a definition can contain. Against Paley, Darwin offered natural selection, a mechanism found in the world. Against “why anything?”, Russell said the universe may just be there. And defenders reply in turn: islands can always be improved, and not everything needs a cause.

cards.headline: Old tools, new puzzles
cards.body: None of this is new equipment. Level 3’s thought experiments, pictured situations reasoned through, are exactly what Zeno’s race and Gaunilo’s island are. And Level 9’s schools already argued over sources of knowledge: Nyaya accepted perception, inference, comparison and testimony, while the Carvakas trusted perception alone.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 complete
learned: How arguments for God start from reason alone or from the world, and how critics answer each.
Why Plato’s cave argues for two worlds, and why Aristotle and Locke rejected them.
How Zeno’s racer seems stuck forever, and how infinite sums reply.
Where Augustine located time once past, future and present seemed to vanish.

questions.prompt: Reality, Time and God recap: what did Kant say about existence, in answer to Anselm?

options.label: It is the greatest perfection of all
options.rationale: That’s what the argument needs, and Kant denies.

options.label: It is not a real predicate
It always needs a first cause
It exists only in the mind
options.rationale: That’s closer to Augustine on time.

questions.explanation: Kant: “Being is evidently not a real predicate”; saying a thing exists adds nothing to its concept.

questions.prompt: Reality, Time and God recap: which character in Hume’s Dialogues says the world resembles an animal more than a watch?

options.label: Cleanthes
options.rationale: In the Dialogues, the line is Philo’s.

questions.explanation: Philo: “the world plainly resembles more an animal or a vegetable, than it does a watch.”

questions.prompt: Reality, Time and God recap: which argument for God starts from reason alone, with no observation?

options.label: Aquinas’s Second Way
options.rationale: It starts from causes we see.

options.label: Al-Ghazali’s argument from beginnings
options.rationale: It starts from the world’s events.

questions.explanation: Ontological arguments proceed from a priori premises alone; cosmological and design arguments start from the observed world.

questions.prompt: Reality, Time and God recap: how did Darwin’s reply to Paley differ from Kant’s reply to Anselm?

options.label: Darwin offered a mechanism in the world; Kant attacked a step of pure reasoning
Darwin attacked the definition of God; Kant offered natural selection
Both argued that the universe is just there
Both accepted the arguments but denied that God is good

questions.explanation: Darwin answered design with natural selection, found in the world; Kant answered Anselm by denying that existence belongs to a concept.

questions.prompt: Reality, Time and God recap: al-Ghazali and Aquinas infer an unseen first cause from causes we observe. Which Level 9 school counted inference as a means of knowledge?

options.label: Only the Buddhists
options.rationale: The level names Nyaya’s four means.

questions.explanation: Nyaya’s four means of knowledge were perception, inference, comparison and testimony.
